title: Roddy McDowall
wiki_lead:
Roderick Andrew Anthony Jude McDowall (17 September 1928 – 3 October 1998) was a British and American actor, with a career spanning six decades on stage and screen. Following early roles as a child star in his native England, he appeared in the American films How Green Was My Valley (1941), My Friend Flicka (1943), and Lassie Come Home (1943). As an adult, McDowall won a Tony Award for his performance in Jean Anouilh's The Fighting Cock (1959–60), played Mordred in the Broadway musical Camelot (1960–61), and was nominated for a Golden Globe for his performance in Cleopatra (1963).
He subsequently appeared in a variety of film and television roles, notably as Cornelius and Caesar in the Planet of the Apes films (1968–73) and Galen in the spin-off television series, as well as The Greatest Story Ever Told (1965), Bedknobs and Broomsticks (1971), The Poseidon Adventure (1972), The Legend of Hell House (1973), The Fantastic Journey (1977), Fright Night (1985), Overboard (1987), A Bug's Life (1998), and as the voice of Jervis Tetch / Mad Hatter in the DC Animated Universe.
McDowall served in various positions on the board of governors for the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences and the selection committee for the Kennedy Center Honors, contributing to various charities related to the film industry and film preservation. He was a founding member of the National Film Preservation Board and represented the Screen Actors Guild on that board until his death. He was also active as a photographer and journalist.

Early life
McDowall was born in Herne Hill, London, the only son of Thomas Andrew McDowall (1896–1978), a merchant seaman, and his Irish wife Winifred (née Corcoran). Both of his parents were enthusiastic about the theatre. McDowall and his elder sister, Virginia, were raised in their mother's Catholic faith. He attended St Joseph's College, Beulah Hill, Upper Norwood, a Roman Catholic secondary school in London.


Career


British films
After appearing as a child model as a baby, and winning an acting prize in a school play at age nine, McDowell started appearing in films, including I See Ice (1938) with George Formby and Hey! Hey! USA (1938) with Will Hay.


Early US films
McDowall and his sister were taken to the United States by their mother after the outbreak of World War II. He became a naturalised United States citizen on 9 December 1949 and lived in the United States for the rest of his life.
McDowall served in the U.S. Army Reserves, and after basic training, was assigned to the 67th Armored Infantry Battalion, 13th Armored Division of the U.S. Army's Organized Reserve Corps headquartered in Los Angeles. Later, he was assigned to the 63rd Infantry Division. McDowall served from 1946 to 1954, spanning from the end of World War II to the end of the Korean War. He then served in the 77th Infantry Division from 1960 to 1962.

grok_lead: Roderick Andrew Anthony Jude McDowall (17 September 1928 â 3 October 1998) was a British-American actor, voice artist, film director, photographer, and film preservationist whose career spanned over six decades and more than 270 screen credits. Born in Herne Hill, London, to merchant seaman Thomas Andrew McDowall and aspiring actress Winifriede Lucinda Corcoran, he began his acting career as a child model and made his film debut at age nine in the British production Murder in the Family (1938). His family relocated to the United States during World War II to escape the Blitz, where he quickly rose to prominence as a child star in Hollywood, portraying young Huw Morgan in John Ford's How Green Was My Valley (1941), which earned five Academy Awards including Best Picture, starring in Lassie Come Home (1943) alongside Elizabeth Taylor, and in My Friend Flicka (1943). As an adult, McDowall transitioned successfully into character roles, gaining iconic status for his portrayal of the intelligent chimpanzee Cornelius in the Planet of the Apes franchise (1968â1973), beginning with the original directed by Franklin J. Schaffner. He also played the young Octavian (later Emperor Augustus) in the epic Cleopatra (1963) opposite Elizabeth Taylor and Richard Burton, and delivered a notable performance as Malcolm in Roman Polanski's Macbeth (1971). Throughout his career, he appeared in over 130 films, numerous Broadway productions such as The Fighting Cock (1960) and The Astrakhan Coat (1967), and television shows, earning a Primetime Emmy Award for his performance in the NBC Sunday Showcase episode "Not Without Honor" (1961). Beyond acting, McDowall was an accomplished still photographer who published five books of celebrity portraits, including Double Exposure, Take One (1990), with proceeds benefiting the Motion Picture & Television Fund, and he amassed a vast personal collection of film memorabilia and rare prints that he donated to the Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences upon his death from lung cancer at age 70 in Studio City, Los Angeles. He was survived by his older sister, Virginia McDowall, a former actress.
